newsitem.title: TANZANIA: IMF expects new aid talks with Tanzania in June.
newsitem.headline: IMF expects new aid talks with Tanzania in June.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is very encouraged by economic reforms in President Benjamin Mkapa's Tanzania and will negotiate a new aid package, IMF Deputy Managing Director Alassane Ouattara said on Tuesday.

Ending a four-day mission to this East African country Ouattara told Reuters the IMF and Tanzania would begin negotiations in June for further aid under the IMF soft-loans Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF).

In November, the IMF approved an ESAF worth $240 million. The funds will be disbursed in six half-yearly instalments starting in January. The new talks are meant to ensure there is no break in the flow of ESAF money.
There was no indication on whether the new ESAF would run alongside that agreed last year or would wait until 1999.
"We are encouraged with the reform progress," Ouattara said, adding that adherence to social and economic reforms meant that the IMF would continue supporting Tanzania's growth efforts.

But he added: "There is still a lot that needs to be done, especially in curbing inflation, balancing the government budget, increasing growth and privatisation of parastatals, including the state-owned National Bank of Commerce (NBC)."

An IMF mission already in Tanzania will evaluate Tanzania's overall performance so far and recommend areas that deserve more attention. Negotiations for the second ESAF will start after the state 1997/98 budget, due on June 19.
"We want to ensure continuity of the facility to enable Tanzania to move ahead with reforms smoothly," Ouattara said.
He said the amount to be negotiated would depend on Tanzania's needs with priority given to education, health and water.
He said the IMF wanted Tanzania's inflation cut to single-digit levels within the next few months as has been projected.
In March, annualised inflation was posted at 17.5 percent, down from over 30 percent some two years ago. Inflation reached a low of 13.8 percent in February, the lowest in a decade.

But failed seasonal short rains in most of East Africa, in October to December last year, and subsequent drought that persisted to March, has forced up food prices and threatens the objective of single-digit inflation.
Food comprises 70 percent of Tanzania's consumer price index basket, according to the treasury.

Ouattara said privatisation of the National Bank of Commerce was a crucial component in economic reforms because more investors would enter the Tanzanian market if they were convinced that the banking system was efficient.

The NBC, created in 1967 as Tanzania started on a path of socialism, holds a 70 percent market share in retail banking. Two years ago, evidence emerged that about 70 percent of its loans portfolio was non-performing and it was engulfed in corruption and undermined by inefficiency.
The government responded by splitting the NBC into three, focusing on business and international trade, medium-sized and regional business and rural banking and urban micro-financing.
Benjamin Mkapa has been in power for around 17 months and is widely credited with attempting to end official corruption, streamline government and free controls on trade.
